## b4b628596579

**A2.** **Reproduced conditional-domain shortcut; target left unchanged.** Inspected
generator SHA-256:
`d0464e7acb1a99276885aae31917fe6cc2a43bd99b1fae40e7f745bbcb040011`;
canonical rule hash: `7f2b54e120ca`.

All canonical examples and all normal generated examples make every later row a
cyclic shift of row 0. Therefore the rival “broadcast row 0 only when every
later row is a cyclic shift; otherwise return the input unchanged” fits the
entire advertised normal generator distribution and all three canonical pairs.
The selected Racket rule itself is broader: it broadcasts row 0 for any
rectangular input.

The exact counterexample at `checks/audit/b4b628596579/input.json` is:

```text
123456
654321
135246
246135
```

It is a dense 4×6 ARC grid, but later rows are not cyclic shifts. The rival
returns it unchanged; the canonical Racket authority broadcasts `123456` to all
four rows, producing 16 differing cells. The supported apply command exited 0
and is retained at `checks/audit/b4b628596579/racket.json`; exact rival output
and cell differences are in `rival.json` and `differences.json`. The current
`self_check` rejects this input with three “not a cyclic shift” errors, so this
is explicitly a **domain restriction/shortcut**, not a validator-accepted bug.
A stronger curriculum would include arbitrary non-top rows because those rows
are semantically irrelevant to the true rule.
